A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same T2DA research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies in v3 limit particular interpretations, but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark returns, component ablations, robustness experiments, embedding visualizations and LoRA comparisons.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and additionally reports BAKU comparisons, training-pipeline ablations and Humanoid results.

M1.justification: The world-model pre-training, contrastive alignment with LoRA and text-conditioned policies remain unchanged. The transformer and diffusion-inference explanations added to Section 3.5 describe procedures already present in v1's Algorithms 4–6 and Appendix D. Joint-training variants are experimental controls.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds evaluation on a simulated humanoid robot benchmark, extending coverage beyond the original navigation, cheetah/ant locomotion and robotic-arm environments. Table 4 also adds handle-pull-side and hand-insert as Meta-World test tasks, but the adjacent text still specifies four test tasks; their actual inclusion is unresolved.

E2.justification: BAKU is added to the Mixed, Expert and Medium comparisons, while DD and DT are removed from those corresponding comparisons. BC-Z, CSRO, UNICORN and AD remain. DD and DT still appear in the new Humanoid comparison, which does not include BAKU.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces controls that jointly train decision embedding and alignment, or all three training stages. The original SAC settings, T2DA hyperparameters and stated evaluation procedures are retained. The conflicting Meta-World test-task count and sparse Humanoid setup prevent establishing their precise evaluation splits.

E4.justification: New Table 9 investigates separate versus joint training on Point-Robot and Meta-World, extending the analysis of training-stage separation. Existing component ablations, data-quality and encoder robustness, LoRA comparisons and embedding visualizations remain. Moving their displays into the main text does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions state five random seeds and 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals for plotted means. However, v3's new training-pipeline and Humanoid return tables report only point estimates, unlike the earlier return tables with uncertainty terms. No change in run counts is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial result groups while retaining all shared tabulated scores. Table 10 reports Humanoid returns of 610.4 and 575.4 for T2DA-T/D versus 531.7 for BC-Z. Table 9 adds Point-Robot returns of -7.2, -8.9 and -16.3 for separate, partially joint and fully joint training. BAKU scores replace DD/DT entries in the established comparisons; these are changes in reported evidence, not demonstrated same-setting T2DA performance gains.

T1.justification: Task assumptions, world-model and contrastive losses, and policy-conditioning mathematics remain equivalent. The transformer-input equation added to the main text already appears in v1's Algorithm 4. No substantive theoretical result, proof or derivation is added.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list and conclusion refine the headline scope from generalist policy learning to offline meta-RL, consistent with v1's already offline setting. The central claims about language grounding, contrastive alignment, two policy architectures and zero-shot generalization remain.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly argues that separate training improves stability and permits independent component replacement or upgrading. Section 5 adds knowledge alignment in VLA models as a future application. Existing interpretations of embedding alignment and limitations concerning small datasets and real-robot deployment remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix D.2 discloses an RTX4080 GPU, Intel i9-10900X CPU, 256 GB RAM, approximately 0.5 hours for pre-training and 0.5–3 hours for policy training. Appendix C adds BAKU's objective and zero-shot adaptation description. Existing architecture details, hyperparameters and implementation links are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises positioning around offline meta-RL and distinguishes T2DA's task representations and conventional policy architectures from VLA policy backbones. It adds discussion of RT-2, OpenVLA, π0.5, BAKU and offline-RL literature, while removing two online LLM-grounding references and the earlier emphasis on text-only or single-task predecessors.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence remains, with targeted rewrites of the framing and related work, fuller explanations in Section 3.5, shortened ablation names and updated affiliations. Appendix material is consolidated into the main narrative and Appendix D gains subsections. An unresolved 'Appendix ??' reference is introduced.

P2.justification: Displays are extensively reorganized: v1's appendix ablation and robustness tables become main-text Tables 2–3, and its Cheetah-Vel visualization becomes Figure 7 in Section 4.4. Several figures adopt text-wrapped layouts. Comparator columns and legends change, and new Tables 9–10 display pipeline and Humanoid results.

improvement.justification: Clearer policy exposition, a relevant BAKU comparison, additional training-pipeline evidence and hardware/timing disclosure modestly improve the paper's assessability. The gain is limited by removal of DD/DT controls from established comparisons, sparse Humanoid documentation, omitted uncertainty in new tables and the contradictory Meta-World test-task count. The revision improves support and explanation without establishing a better underlying method or higher retained performance.
